story.title: An answer can be fluent and still fail to explain the question
paragraphs: A forward language model scores how plausible a response is after a prompt, but a plausible continuation can quietly drop one of the problem’s constraints. LEDOM asks the complementary question: given the response, how well can a model reconstruct the prompt? The intended signal is sensitivity to the premises, not fluency.

Both factorization directions are exact by the chain rule, but with finite data and capacity they learn different approximations. LEDOM isolates the asymmetry: reverse and forward models share the architecture, the tokenizer and a 435B-token corpus of general text, mathematics and code, at 2B and 7B parameters. The public 7B checkpoint (Reverse-Model-7B-348B) is a preliminary release at about 348B training tokens, according to the code repository.

mechanism.title: Reconstruct the prompt, then combine the two scores
paragraphs: For a question x and a candidate response y, the forward model estimates P(y | x); the reverse model reads the reversed response, then the reversed prompt, and estimates P(x | y). The prompt tokens are what is scored, so the method does not ask a second model whether an answer looks correct.

Reverse Reward combines the two as P(y | x)^(1−λ) × P(x | y)^λ, a weighted sum of log-likelihoods. The paper’s Proposition 1 states when this helps: an incorrect chain with comparable forward likelihood but poorer backward reconstruction is ranked lower.

The main experiments rerank 64 sampled complete responses; a step-level beam search scores partial paths. The forward generator is unchanged, the reverse scorer is fine-tuned on math data, and each candidate costs one extra reverse forward pass.

evidence.title: Reverse scores choose better answers than greedy or random selection
paragraphs: In the paper’s download case, a 200 GB file at 2 GB/minute fails at 40% and needs a 20-minute restart and a fresh download: 40 + 20 + 100 = 160 minutes. The forward model’s top candidate downloads only the remainder and adds a second restart; Reverse Reward ranks it lower because that chain cannot reconstruct the problem.

Random selection from the same samples is usually below greedy decoding, so the gain comes from the reverse score, not from sampling diversity. Finer search is not always better: on AIME 2024, OpenMath2’s step-level beam search falls below greedy decoding, which the paper attributes to pruning partially correct beams early.

reading_notes: Re-read §§2,5,6,Limitations,Tables 2–4 and 7–8, Appendices B–D. Explicitly correct no-training ambiguity: forward weights unchanged, RLM fine-tuned on mathematical reasoning data (§6.1). v5 demos use only published material: reverse-generation outputs from Table 2 and Appendix Figures 5–6 (word-level order marked illustrative) and the measured Table 4 comparison. The paper prints no per-candidate reverse scores or λ, so no per-candidate probabilities are shown.

demo.provenance: Method: five reverse-generation examples as printed in Table 2, Appendix B Figure 5 and Appendix C Figure 6, replayed word by word from the end (illustrative order). Evidence: Reverse Reward accuracies from Table 4. The paper reports no per-candidate forward or reverse scores (Tables 7-8 give responses and orderings only), so none are shown or invented.
